title: Diverse AI Personas Can Mitigate the Homogenization Effect in Human-AI Collaborative Ideation
pub: arXiv:2504.13868 [cs.HC]; accepted and forthcoming in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
author: Yun Wan · Yoram M. Kalman

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

st.t: Task allocation: AI redistributes skill and responsibility
st.an: The EntityClusterSummary contains no title, description, key points or quotations. There is therefore insufficient evidence to determine the source's position on the cluster's proposition that AI's effects depend on task allocation and governance-sensitive deployment.

st.t: Creative diversity: Individual gains can homogenise groups
st.an: The source accepts the distinction between improved individual creativity and reduced collective diversity, then materially extends it by testing diversified AI personas as a mitigation strategy. Its results are explicitly preliminary: low statistical power and unresolved preservation of individual creativity gains support the cluster’s treatment of personas as promising but unproven.
qs: e most prominent of these studies is Doshi and Hauser's (2024) paper which demonstrated that GenAI-generated plot ideas enhanced the creativity of individual storywriters but, notably, reduced the collective diversity of their stories.

Our study achieved only 55.4% power to detect the observed eﬀects, and the small eﬀect sizes (Cohen's f = 0.244) mean that we cannot conclusively distinguish between genuine enhancement and random variation.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: Accepts the cluster’s conditional, workflow-dependent framing and materially extends it to creative diversity: homogenization may result from uniform deployment rather than GenAI itself, while prompt variation and configurable personas may preserve collective creativity. The supplied excerpt offers design implications but no methods or quantitative comparison establishing their effectiveness.
qs: the trade-oﬀ may emerge from uniform deployment practices rather than from an inherent limitation of GenAI, and that diversity can be intentionally built into AI-mediated collaboration.
Our study highlights the risks of over-standardization, the importance of prompt variation, and the value of treating GenAI not as a static tool but as a conﬁgurable partner.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s interaction-design claim by experimentally showing that differentiated AI personas can produce more varied inputs and may preserve collective diversity in human–AI creative work. It reinforces the view that outcomes depend on configured workflows rather than model access alone, while its underpowered human phase limits generalisation, especially to legal work.
qs: e implication is that eﬀective human-AI collaboration requires researchers and practitioners to make their implicit assumptions about diversity, perspective, and variation explicit in their interaction design, treating AI not as an intuitive collaborator who can extract implicit unstated needs, but as a powerful tool that excels at delivering precisely what is speciﬁed.

These findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept that persona-based approaches can prevent the homogenization effect, with replication in larger samples needed for definitive conclusions about diversity enhancement.

st.t: Creative personas: Diversity advantage remains unmeasured
st.an: The source aligns closely with the synthesis: it presents differentiated personas and temperature adjustment as design variables, documents a benchmark-comparison setup, and supplies illustrative plots, but the supplied evidence does not report comparative results demonstrating that personas reduce homogenisation.

kp.k: Homogenization may reflect deployment choices rather than inherent limitations
kp.d: Wan and Kalman investigate creative storywriting, not legal services. They argue that uniform AI inputs can narrow the collective creative space even when individual users benefit. Their two-phase experiment provides initial, qualified evidence that intentionally diversified inputs can mitigate homogenization; they frame AI configuration, rather than AI assistance alone, as consequential.
qs: Our ﬁndings suggest that the trade-oﬀ may emerge from uniform deployment practices rather than from an inherent limitation of GenAI, and that diversity can be intentionally built into AI-mediated collaboration.

kp.k: Prior research distinguishes individual gains from collective convergence
kp.d: The authors report that Doshi and Hauser (2024) found improved individual story creativity but increased cosine similarity of 10.7% and 8.9% with access to one or five AI plot ideas. They also report higher-quality but less diverse consulting solutions in Dell’Acqua et al. (2023), and semantic similarity increases of 60% and 32% for AI ghostwriting and reviewing advertising copy respectively in Chen and Chan (2024). These are findings attributed to earlier studies, not results of the present experiment.
qs: is was evidenced by the cosine similarity scores rising by 10.7% and 8.9% for participants with access to one or ﬁve GenAI plot ideas, respectively.

In another study Boston Consulting Group consultants using GenAI were found to generate more solutions to client problems and these solutions were rated as higher quality, but according to their semantic similarity metrics, the diversity of solutions decreased (Dell’Acqua et al., 2023).

kp.k: Uniform prompting creates shared creative reference points
kp.d: The authors propose that ideas novel to each individual can nevertheless homogenize a collection when similar ideas reach everyone. They interpret identical prompting in Doshi and Hauser’s design as effectively assigning the same AI collaborator to every participant. This is their explanation of the mechanism, rather than a claim that individual originality and collective diversity are interchangeable.
qs: However, when this same “novelty” is uniformly distributed across diﬀerent participants, it creates a shared reference point that constrains the collective creative space.
All participants in these experiments essentially collaborated with identical AI partners, despite working on individual creative tasks.

kp.k: Ten personas generated a deliberately diversified plot pool
kp.d: Phase 1 used ChatGPT o1-preview to develop ten personas across 14 trait categories, including cultural background, cognitive styles and literary preferences, excluding adventure preferences. GPT-4o version 2024-05-13 on Azure OpenAI generated 31 plots per persona, retaining the first 30 for a 300-plot pool. Plots were three-sentence adventures on another planet. Temperature was raised from 0.7 to 0.9 after redundant outputs; top P was 1. A separate comparison set comprised 30 GPT-4 outputs from the earlier study’s uniform prompt.
qs: Using this framework, we then prompted the model to generate 10 detailed persona proﬁles of at least 100 words each.
ese personas were incorporated into an assistant on the Azure OpenAI platform using gpt-4o version 2024-05-13, temperature=0.9, top P = 1.
is phenomenon was resolved when the temperature was raised from 0.7 to 0.9.

kp.k: Between-persona plots showed lower semantic similarity
kp.d: Using text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings with 1,536 dimensions, the authors compared 4,350 within-persona pairs and 40,500 between-persona pairs. On similarity scores scaled to 100, within-persona similarity averaged 87.41 (SD 3.17), versus 82.93 (SD 3.12) between personas; the reported difference was 4.49, t = 119.9443, p < 0.00000001, Cohen’s d = 1.4254. The uniform-prompt comparison averaged 90.99 (SD 2.78). The authors attribute relatively high absolute similarities partly to shared genre, format and model foundations.
qs: Our analysis demonstrates robust persona distinctiveness in AI persona-generated plots, with mean intra-persona similarity of 87.41 (SD = 3.17) signiﬁcantly exceeding inter-persona similarity of 82.93 (SD = 3.12).

First, all personas were constrained to generate content within the same genre (adventure stories set on other planets) and format (exactly three sentences), creating structural similarities that elevate baseline similarity scores.

kp.k: Persona distinctiveness varied substantially across configurations
kp.d: All ten personas had positive distinctiveness scores, defined as mean within-persona minus mean between-persona similarity. Carlos, combining Caribbean background, comedy and divergent thinking, scored highest at 7.69; Elena, combining North American background, graphic novels and holistic thinking, scored lowest at 2.48. The authors suggest humor and divergent thinking may differentiate outputs, while some traits may align with prevalent training-data patterns; these trait-level explanations are speculative.
qs: With scores ranging from 2.48 to 7.69, this distribution demonstrates that while all personas achieved meaningful diﬀerentiation, there is substantial room for optimization in persona design.

e divergent thinking style might also have contributed to Persona 6’s distinctiveness by generating unexpected plot developments and creative solutions that deviate from conventional adventure narrative structures.

kp.k: Human experiment tested optional access to diversified plots
kp.d: Phase 2 recruited 100 UK-based Prolific participants using the earlier study’s criteria: approval ratings at or above 95% and 100 to 1,000,000 prior submissions. Participants were randomly assigned to write eight-sentence stories without AI plots, with optional access to one plot, or with optional access to up to five randomly selected plots. Excluding three control participants who reported external AI use left 97 stories: 32 control, 33 one-plot and 32 five-plot. Access did not require requesting or using ideas.
qs: In line with Doshi and Hauser, participants could choose whether to ask for plots or not, and were not required to use the plot ideas even if they requested them.

Aer excluding data from three participants in the control group who reported using external AI to inspire their stories, we analyzed 97 stories: 32 in the control group, 33 in the 1-plot condition, and 32 in the 5-plot condition.

kp.k: Centroid analysis detected no significant condition differences
kp.d: Replicating the earlier study’s story-to-group-centroid method, mean similarity was 90.588 for control, 90.095 for one plot and 90.233 for five plots. Relative to control, coefficients were −0.493 (p = 0.301) and −0.356 (p = 0.459); ANOVA gave F(2, 94) = 0.573, p = 0.57. The authors emphasize that this analysis did not reproduce the statistically significant homogenization previously reported.
qs: e replication analysis results indicated no signiﬁcant diﬀerence in story similarity across conditions (1-plot condition: b = -0.493, p = 0.301; 5-plot condition: b = -0.356, p = 0.459, see Table 2).

kp.k: One-plot diversity enhancement depended on analytical approach
kp.d: A mixed-effects model accounting for repeated appearances of stories in 1,520 pairwise comparisons found lower similarity for one plot versus control: β = −1.073, 95% CI [−1.971, −0.175], p = 0.019. Five plots showed a nonsignificant reduction: β = −0.488, 95% CI [−1.394, 0.418], p = 0.291. Story-level ANOVA was nonsignificant, F(2, 94) = 2.33, p = 0.103; the control-versus-one-plot comparison gave p = 0.064, and a 10,000-iteration permutation test gave p = 0.113. The authors describe enhancement as proof-of-concept requiring replication.
qs: The 1-plot condition showed statistically significant evidence of enhanced diversity relative to the human-only baseline, while the 5-plot condition showed a similar but non-significant pattern.

These findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept that persona-based approaches can prevent the homogenization effect, with replication in larger samples needed for definitive conclusions about diversity enhancement.

kp.k: Bayesian findings do not establish definitive equivalence
kp.d: Bayesian estimated differences versus control were −0.88, 95% HDI [−1.69, −0.04], for one plot and −0.63, 95% HDI [−1.49, 0.20], for five plots. With a ±0.5-point region of practical equivalence, 68.2% of the posterior for the two assisted conditions fell inside the region. BF₀₁ values were 0.55 for one plot versus control, 1.72 for five plots versus control and 3.97 between assisted conditions. The authors characterize control comparisons as inconclusive or weak and acknowledge that practical equivalence is not proven.
qs: e Bayesian analysis, while providing moderate evidence against large diﬀerences between conditions, does not constitute deﬁnitive proof of equivalence.

e inconclusive Bayes factors for comparisons with the control condition (BF₀₁ = 0.55 for 1-plot, BF₀₁ = 1.72 for 5-plot) indicate that our data do not strongly favor either the null hypothesis or the alternative.

kp.k: AI-assisted stories contained richer descriptive and emotional language
kp.d: NLTK analysis combining both assisted conditions found higher descriptive-word means, 18.321 versus 15.854, and emotional-word means, 8.018 versus 6.829, than human-only stories. Tests gave t = −2.434, p = 0.017 and t = −2.592, p = 0.011 respectively. Other listed linguistic measures did not reach p < 0.05, and neither assisted condition significantly differed from the other. The authors interpret these findings as linguistic enrichment alongside preserved semantic diversity.
qs: Our analysis revealed that AI-assisted stories featured greater diversity in descriptive words (t = -2.434, p = 0.017) and emotional words (t = -2.592, p = 0.011) compared to human-only stories (Table 5).
ere were no signiﬁcant diﬀerences between AI-assisted 1-plot and 5-plot stories (Table 6).

kp.k: Limited power and unmeasured creativity gains constrain conclusions
kp.d: The authors report 55.4% achieved power for observed Cohen’s f = 0.244, compared with 96.9% for the earlier study’s n = 293, and estimate approximately 165 participants, 55 per condition, for 80% power at their observed effect. They explicitly leave unresolved whether diversified inputs preserve the individual creativity gains found previously. They call for larger and additional populations, other models, languages and contexts, adaptive diversity controls and less computationally costly approaches.
qs: Prospective power calculations indicate that detecting our observed effect at 80% power would require approximately 165 total participants (55 per condition).
Whether the individual creativity gains documented by Doshi and Hauser (2024) are maintained under diversiﬁed conditions remains an important question for future research.

kp.k: Design for varied perspectives and collective outcomes
kp.d: The authors recommend avoiding homogeneous deployment and treating diversity as an explicit design objective alongside individual performance. They identify personas as one approach among cultural and disciplinary variation, cognitive styles, multi-model ensembles, dynamic randomization and simulated team roles. They acknowledge that persona effects on accuracy, bias and refusals are unpredictable in other research. Their broader recommendations include examining long-term aided and unaided creativity, fixation and intrinsic motivation; these extend beyond the outcomes directly tested here.
qs: Our persona-based approach represents just one solution among many for applying this established principle to human-AI collaboration.
e results of these studies do not argue against personas; they argue for purposeful use.
For researchers, they suggest that diversity should be treated not as a byproduct, but as a core design principle in human-GenAI creative tasks.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wan and Kalman claim that intentionally diversified AI plot ideas can mitigate homogenization in human–AI collaborative storytelling, preserving collective diversity and potentially enhancing it.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about creative ideation, not legal services. The authors argue that homogenization may result from uniform deployment and prompting rather than an inherent limitation of generative AI. They present diverse AI personas as one way to vary creative inputs. Their experiment provides initial evidence of diversity preservation, with enhancement most apparent in the one-plot condition. They also report richer descriptive and emotional language in AI-assisted stories. Their broader design implication is that organizations should intentionally diversify AI contributions rather than standardize every user's creative inputs. They do not establish that the individual creativity improvements reported in prior research persist under their diversified conditions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their claims with a two-phase experiment combining AI plot generation, randomized human storytelling conditions, semantic similarity measures, and linguistic analysis.
pts.d: Phase 1 generated 300 plots across 10 personas using GPT-4o. Mean within-persona similarity was 87.41 and between-persona similarity was 82.93, on a scale multiplied by 100; the authors report Cohen's d = 1.4254. A separate set of 30 plots generated with a uniform GPT-4 prompt had mean similarity of 90.99. Phase 2 recruited 100 UK-based Prolific participants and analyzed 97 stories after excluding three control participants who reported external AI assistance. The final groups comprised 32 human-only participants, 33 offered one plot, and 32 offered up to five plots. Centroid-based regression and ANOVA found no significant condition differences. Mixed-effects analysis found significantly lower similarity for the one-plot condition versus control (β = -1.073, p = 0.019), but not for the five-plot condition (β = -0.488, p = 0.291). Story-level ANOVA and permutation testing were nonsignificant. Linguistic analysis found higher descriptive-word and emotional-word measures in the combined AI-assisted groups (p = 0.017 and p = 0.011). The authors report only 55.4% achieved power and characterize the findings as proof of concept rather than definitive evidence of diversity enhancement. Their explanation of homogenization also draws on prior studies, which are supporting literature rather than findings from this experiment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern immediate outcomes in a bounded storytelling experiment; broader and longer-term effects remain prospective and conditional.
pts.d: The 2025 paper does not forecast a date for industry transformation. Participants wrote eight-sentence stories about adventures on another planet, with optional access to pre-generated three-sentence plots randomly selected from a diversified pool. Requesting or using the plots was not compulsory. Personas were developed using o1-preview, and persona plots used GPT-4o version 2024-05-13, temperature 0.9 and top P 1. These were satisficing design choices rather than demonstrated optimal settings. The authors qualify diversity enhancement because of limited statistical power and call for larger samples, additional populations, models, languages, contexts, and adaptive diversity controls. Their proposed creative-catalyst mechanism and discussion of agentic collaboration are interpretations and future design possibilities, not demonstrations of autonomous multi-step systems. Whether diversified assistance maintains individual creativity gains, or changes creativity over the medium and long term, remains open.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected group is human storytellers using AI inspiration; the proposed implications extend to creative practitioners, organizations, researchers, and human–AI system designers.
pts.d: For individual writers, diversified AI ideas may stimulate distinct narratives and richer language. For groups of creators, varying inputs may protect the collective range of ideas even when each participant works individually. For organizations and system designers, the authors advocate avoiding homogeneous deployment and considering collective diversity alongside individual performance. For researchers, they recommend treating diversity as an explicit design objective and studying outcomes beyond immediate task performance. These are implications for creative collaboration, not findings about lawyers, law firms, legal clients, legal markets, or access to justice.
